findings.title: A2A Java SDK: Android synchronous POST forwards credentials across authorities after incomplete redirect fix
findings.summary:
The GHSA-9rhm fix added this safe setting in
AndroidA2AHttpClient.createConnection():

    connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(false);

The synchronous POST builder later overwrites it:

    private boolean followRedirects = true;

    public A2AHttpResponse post() throws IOException {
        HttpURLConnection connection = createConnection("POST", false);
        connection.setInstanceFollowRedirects(followRedirects);
        // ...
    }

The second assignment wins. JSONRPCTransport and RestTransport both
add interceptor-produced headers and call synchronous post() without
setting followRedirects(false).

On Android's repackaged OkHttp implementation, a cross-authority
redirect strips Authorization but retains nonstandard request headers.
AuthInterceptor permits four nonstandard authentication header names:

    X-API-Key
    API-Key
    X-Auth-Token
    X-Authentication

I confirmed that the exact v1.3.1.Final Maven artifact forwards
complete synthetic values under all four names to a second loopback
authority. I also reproduced the supported AuthInterceptor to Android
POST path. Explicitly calling followRedirects(false) returns the
original 302 and produces no request to the collector.

All test traffic stayed on two ephemeral 127.0.0.1 listeners. All
credentials were synthetic FULCRUM-SYNTHETIC-* values.

Reproduction

I have attached AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest.java. Copy it to:

    extras/http-client-android/src/test/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/client/http/android/

Run:

    mvn -pl extras/http-client-android -am \
      -Dtest=AndroidA2AHttpClientRedirectTest \
      -Dsurefire.failIfNoSpecifiedTests=false test

On unpatched current main, the default test fails with:

    Android synchronous POST must retain the documented no-redirect default
    expected: <302> but was: <200>

The explicit followRedirects(true) control still passes.

The separate exact-artifact fixture passed three consecutive runs. Its
relevant output was:

    default status=200 x-ap

findings.title: AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web
findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? Proactive monitoring at Google The landscape of IPI on the web There are many channels through which attackers might try to send prompt injections. However, one location is particularly easy to observe - the public web. Here, threat actors may simply seed prompt injections on websites in hope of corrupting AI systems that browse them. findings.title: Google Workspace’s continuous approach to mitigating indirect prompt injections
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. That’s why Google takes a sophisticated and comprehensive approach to these attacks. We’re continuously improving LLM resistance to IPI attacks and launching AI application capabilities with ever-improving defenses. Staying ahead of the latest indirect prompt injection attacks is critical to our mission of securing Workspace with Gemini. In our previous blog “ Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy ”, we reviewed the layered architecture of our IPI defenses. In this blog, we’ll share more detail on the continuous approach we take to improve these defenses and to solve for new attacks. New attack discovery By proactively discovering and cataloging new attack vectors through internal and external programs, we can identify vulnerabilities and deploy robust defenses ahead of adversarial activity. Human Red-Teaming Human Red-Teaming uses adversarial simulations to uncover security and safety vulnerabilities. Specialized teams execute attacks based on realistic user profiles to exploit weaknesses, coordinating with product teams to resolve identified issues. Automated Red-Teaming Automated Red-Teaming is done via dynamic, machine-learning-driven frameworks to stress-test environments. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. Checking agent outputs with User Alignment Critic The main planning model for Gemini uses page content shared in Chrome to decide what action to take next. findings.title: Rust in Android: move fast and fix things
findings.summary: Posted by Jeff Vander Stoep, Android Last year, we wrote about why a memory safety strategy that focuses on vulnerability prevention in new code quickly yields durable and compounding gains. This year we look at how this approach isn’t just fixing things, but helping us move faster . The 2025 data continues to validate the approach, with memory safety vulnerabilities falling below 20% of total vulnerabilities for the first time. Updated data for 2025. This data covers first-party and third-party (open source) code changes to the Android platform across C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Rust. This post is published a couple of months before the end of 2025, but Android’s industry-standard 90-day patch window means that these results are very likely close to final. We can and will accelerate patching when necessary. We adopted Rust for its security and are seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android’s C and C++ code . But the biggest surprise was Rust's impact on software delivery. With Rust changes having a 4x lower rollback rate and spending 25% less time in code review , the safer path is now also the faster one. In this post, we dig into the data behind this shift and also cover: How we’re expanding our reach: We're pushing to make secure code the default across our entire software stack. We have updates on Rust adoption in first-party apps, the Linux kernel, and firmware. Our first rust memory safety vulnerability...almost: We'll analyze a near-miss memory safety bug in unsafe Rust: how it happened, how it was mitigated, and steps we're taking to prevent recurrence. It’s also a good chance to answer the question “if Rust can have memory safety issues, why bother at all?” Building Better Software, Faster Developing an operating system requires the low-level control and predictability of systems programming languages like C, C++, and Rust. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. findings.title: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite
findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. findings.title: A2A Java SDK: Push notification credentials logged in cleartext on protobuf parse failure
findings.summary:
### *Impact.** Push notification bearer tokens and authentication credentials submitted by clients are written to server log files in cleartext. Any operator, log aggregation system, or attacker with log access can read these secrets and use them to authenticate to the client's push notification endpoints, potentially sending forged task status updates.

**Where.** `transport/rest/src/main/java/org/a2aproject/sdk/transport/rest/handler/RestHandler.java:676` in `parseRequestBody`

**What.** The `parseRequestBody` method logs the entire JSON request body at `SEVERE` level when `JsonFormat.parser().merge()` throws `InvalidProtocolBufferException`. This method is called from `createTaskPushNotificationConfiguration` (line 377), where the body contains client-supplied push notification bearer tokens (field `token`) and authentication credentials (field `authentication.credentials`). These secrets are written to server log files in full.

**Exploit scenario.** A client creates a push notification configuration by POSTing to `/v1/tenants/{tenant}/tasks/{taskId}/pushNotificationConfigs` with a body containing `{"url": "https://client.example.com/webhook", "token": "secret-bearer-token", "authentication": {"scheme": "Bearer", "credentials": "oauth-access-token"}, "extraField": "value"}`. The extra field causes `JsonFormat.parser().merge()` to throw `InvalidProtocolBufferException`. The entire body including `secret-bearer-token` and `oauth-access-token` is logged at SEVERE level. An attacker with log access retrieves the cleartext credentials.

**Preconditions.**
- Attacker must have access to server log files (centralized logging, log aggregation, shared infrastructure, or insider access)
- Push notification capability must be enabled
- A request body must fail protobuf deserialization while being valid JSON (unknown fields with strict parsing, schema mismatches)

**Fix.** Do not log the raw request body. Log only a sanitized summary — body length and content type, not cont

findings.title: A2A Java SDK has Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) in push-notification delivery
findings.summary:
---

- **Ecosystem:** Maven
- **Affected package:** `org.a2aproject.sdk:a2a-java-sdk-server-common` (push-notification delivery)
- **Affected versions:** `<= 1.2.0.Final` (and `1.2.1.Final-SNAPSHOT` on `main` prior to the fix)
- **Patched version:** _(the release that carries the fix)_
- **CWE:** CWE-918 (Server-Side Request Forgery)
- **Severity:** High
- **CVSS v3.1:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:L/A:N` (5.8, Moderate)

---

## Summary

An **unauthenticated** attacker can coerce the a2a-java server into issuing HTTP requests to
arbitrary internal and cloud-metadata endpoints from the server's own network position — a
Server-Side Request Forgery reachable in the default deployment with no credentials, no user
interaction, and a single request. The behaviour is the shipped default, not a misconfiguration.

## Details

`BasePushNotificationSender` (in `server-common`) POSTs task data to the URL stored on a task's
`TaskPushNotificationConfig` with no validation of the destination: no block on loopback, RFC1918,
link-local (`169.254.0.0/16`, including the `169.254.169.254` metadata address), unique-local,
unspecified, or multicast ranges; no scheme restriction; and no bound on redirects.
`InMemoryPushNotificationConfigStore.setInfo` stores the URL verbatim and
`onCreateTaskPushNotificationConfig` does not check it either.

Both shipped HTTP clients follow redirects (`JdkA2AHttpClient` → `followRedirects(NORMAL)`,
`VertxA2AHttpClient` → `setFollowRedirects(true)`), so a creation-time URL allowlist is bypassable:
an attacker webhook answers `302 Location: http://169.254.169.254/...` and the client follows it. A
hostname check is likewise defeated by DNS rebinding. A correct guard must validate the *resolved*
IP of every hop at connection time, not the URL string.

## Exploitation

Demonstrated end-to-end against a running server (default wiring, unauthenticated caller):

- **Arbitrary internal reachability.** The attacker picks the destination and the server

findings.title: Pillow: OOB read in TiffDecode.c tile and RGBA paths leaks heap memory into pixels
findings.summary:
```
============================================================================
OOB read in TiffDecode.c tile and RGBA paths leaks heap memory into pixels
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:483  in _decodeTile()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

Pillow reads past the end of a heap buffer when decoding certain malformed compressed TIFF files, and copies the bytes it reads into the pixels of the image it returns. An attacker who can get an application to open and load an image file, for example by uploading it to a service that returns thumbnails, previews or converted images, gets back fragments of that process's heap memory, including pointer values. A slightly larger file instead crashes the process. No special settings are needed, and nothing is written out of bounds.

The bug is in `_decodeTile()` and `_decodeAsRGBA()` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. Both size their decode buffer from libtiff's view of the pixel layout (`TIFFTileSize()`/`TIFFTileRowSize()`, or `img.width * 4`). They then unpack each row with the unpacker that `TiffImagePlugin._setup()` chose from Pillow's own parse of the directory, and neither checks that the unpacker's input row fits inside the row libtiff produced. `_decodeStrip()` has exactly this check, added for OSS-Fuzz `crash-0da0` in 8.2.0, but the tile and RGBA paths never got it.

The two parsers can be made to disagree with a duplicated `PhotometricInterpretation` or `BitsPerSample` tag, because libtiff keeps the first occurrence and Pillow keeps the last. Pillow then unpacks 4 to 8 bytes per pixel from rows that libtiff filled with 1 to 4 bytes, so the last rows of each tile are read from beyond the buffer. The disclosed memory is a few tile rows past the buffer, and the attacker chooses the tile width. The amount does not grow with the number of tiles, because the buffer is reused for every tile.

The tile half was introduced in

findings.title: markdown-it: Quadratic-time rendering of a single multi-line link reference definition with default options (regression since 14.0)
findings.summary:
### Summary

A link reference definition whose label or title is never closed is O(n²) in markdown-it 15.0.2 with default options. Continuation lines are pulled lazily with str += lineContent in src/rules_block/reference.ts, and the subsequent charCodeAt and slice calls flatten the V8 cons-string, copying everything collected so far; this runs before the rule decides the definition is invalid. It is a regression introduced by PR #1004 in 14.0.0: 13.0.2 processed a 313 KB input in 125 ms, while every version since takes about 11 seconds on the same input. At the sizes below, 200 KB takes 3.6 seconds, 400 KB takes 18.1 seconds, and 800 KB takes 74.0 seconds, which is roughly 4–5× per doubling. No options are required to trigger it.

### Details

src/rules_block/reference.ts appends continuation lines with str += lineContent at lines 74, 83, 100, 133, and 150, then keeps indexing the accumulated string via str.charCodeAt(pos) in the label and whitespace loops and str.slice(...) in parseLinkTitle. V8 represents += as a cons-string, and the next charCodeAt or slice flattens it, copying everything collected so far, so one definition spanning n lines costs O(n²). Isolation confirms the rule is responsible: block-only parsing with inline disabled is still quadratic, md.disable('reference') makes the same input linear, and the same text without the leading [ is linear. The fix is to track positions in state.src instead of building str, or to collect line slices in an array and parse across them. At minimum, stop scanning the label after 999 characters (CommonMark §6.3) before pulling more lines, and cap title continuation. Add a pathological test with a 100k-line unclosed title and label. Open PR #1215 edits the same file but its label check runs after the label loop, so it does not bound either variant and the fix can land together with that PR.

The observed output from PoC was:
unclosed title n=100000   200009 B    3585.5 ms
unclosed title n=200000   400009 B   18107.1 ms

findings.title: markdown-it: Quadratic-time denial of service in inline HTML parsing with html enabled
findings.summary:
### Summary

With `html: true`, markdown-it takes quadratic time to parse repeated unterminated HTML constructs inside a paragraph. This affects HTML comments (`<!--`), processing instructions (`<?`), declarations (`<!A`), and CDATA sections (`<![CDATA[`).

An attacker-controlled input of a few hundred kilobytes can block the Node.js event loop for seconds or tens of seconds. The default configuration has HTML disabled, but the `commonmark` preset enables it.

The issue was reported against the published `markdown-it@15.0.2` package on Node.js 20 and reproduced on the current source with Node.js 24.16.0.

### Details

`src/rules_inline/text.ts` treats `<` as a terminator, causing the inline parser to attempt the HTML rule at successive HTML construct openers.

With HTML enabled, `src/rules_inline/html_inline.ts` applies an anchored regular expression to the remaining input:

```js
const match = state.src.slice(pos).match(HTML_TAG_RE)
```

The comment, processing instruction, declaration, and CDATA alternatives in `src/common/html_re.ts` scan the remaining input for their respective terminators: `-->`, `?>`, `>`, and `]]>`.

When the terminator is absent, matching fails. Parsing eventually reaches the next opener and scans an overlapping suffix again. Repeating this across the paragraph produces quadratic total work. For these inputs, the problem is repeated scanning across separate matches.

The payload must reach inline parsing. Prefixing it with `x ` keeps it inside a paragraph. Starting a line directly with one of these constructs instead invokes HTML block parsing, which does not exhibit the same repeated inline scans for these payloads.

The existing `unclosed <!--` test in `test/markdown-it/pathological.test.mjs` already contains a reproducer:

```js
'</' + '<!--'.repeat(100000)
```

However, it runs with default options, where HTML is disabled.

A fix should avoid repeated searches for absent terminators across all four affected alternatives, for example by c

findings.title: MCP  TypeScript server SDK: Shared transport or server instances delivered one HTTP client's messages to another
findings.summary:
### Summary
In affected versions, an MCP server reached over HTTP could deliver one client's responses and notifications to another client. This happened when clients shared one stateless transport, or one `McpServer` or `Server` instance.

Messages were matched to a connection by JSON-RPC `id` alone. SDK clients number requests from 0, so ids collide in normal use.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if more than one client can reach your HTTP endpoint and your code creates the transport or the server once at startup, instead of once per request or per session. Until this release, the README examples of `@modelcontextprotocol/hono`, `express`, `fastify` and `node` showed that pattern.

Affected versions: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0.

Not affected:

- `createMcpHandler()` with a factory that builds a new server on every call
- stdio servers
- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.26.0 and later

### Fix
Upgrade to `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.0 or later.

**You also need to change your code.** The SDK now refuses to be shared, so an affected app fails requests after upgrading: a second `connect()` rejects with `ALREADY_CONNECTED`, and a stateless transport rejects its second request.

Change to one of these:

- **`createMcpHandler()`:** pass a factory that builds a new `McpServer` on every call.
- **Per request:** build a new `McpServer` and a new transport inside the request handler.
- **Per session:** set `sessionIdGenerator` and keep one `McpServer` and one transport per session.

If you cannot upgrade yet, the same change fixes affected versions.

findings.title: MCP TypeScript SDK: Server bearer authentication accepted tokens issued for another service
findings.summary:
### Summary
In affected versions, the SDK's server-side bearer authentication had no way to check that a token was issued for your server (its audience). Where one authorization server issues tokens for several services, a valid token for another service was also accepted by your MCP server.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if your HTTP server uses `requireBearerAuth()` or `verifyBearerToken()`, its authorization server also issues tokens for other services, and your `verifyAccessToken()` does not check the token's audience (`aud`) itself.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.6.0 through 1.31.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/express` 2.0.0 through 2.0.1
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server-legacy` 2.0.0 through 2.3.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.0 or later, together with `@modelcontextprotocol/express` 2.0.2 or later if you use it
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server-legacy` 2.3.1 or later

**Upgrading alone changes nothing.** The patched versions add an `expectedResource` setting that is off by default. To turn the check on, make both of these changes together:

1. Pass the audience your authorization server puts in tokens for your server: `requireBearerAuth({ verifier, expectedResource: new URL('https://mcp.example.com/mcp') })`.
2. Return the token's audience from `verifyAccessToken()` as `AuthInfo.resource`, also a `URL`.

A token for another service then gets `401`. With only the first change, every request gets `401`.

If you cannot upgrade yet, reject any token whose `aud` does not include your server inside `verifyAccessToken()`. That closes the issue on every version.

findings.title: MCP TypeScript client SDK: HTTP client transports and OAuth requests followed cross-origin redirects and re-sent custom headers and request bodies
findings.summary:
### Summary
In affected versions, the SDK's HTTP client transports and OAuth requests followed redirects to any origin.

If an MCP server or authorization server redirected a request to another origin, that origin received custom request headers (such as an `X-API-Key` set in `requestInit.headers`) and the `mcp-session-id` header. On a `307` or `308` it also received the request body, including OAuth token requests with their `refresh_token` and `client_secret`.

On current runtimes `fetch` already drops the `Authorization` header across origins.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if your application uses `StreamableHTTPClientTransport`, `SSEClientTransport`, or the SDK's OAuth client functions such as `auth()`. stdio clients are not affected.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` all versions through 1.31.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.3.0 or later

Redirects are now followed only within the same origin, and not at all in browsers. If your MCP server or authorization server redirects to another origin on purpose, configure the final URL instead. Setting `redirectPolicy: 'follow'` on a transport restores the old behaviour and the exposure.

If a redirect may have reached a host you do not control, rotate the API keys and `client_secret` your application held and revoke its tokens.

If you cannot upgrade yet, pass a `fetch` that refuses redirects, for example `(url, init) => fetch(url, { ...init, redirect: 'error' })`.

findings.title: ApostropheCMS uploadfs Azure backend leaks account-level SAS token into every public attachment URL (sas: true)
findings.summary:
## Summary

When uploadfs is configured with the Azure backend and `sas: true` (a supported configuration introduced in uploadfs 1.25.0), `createContainer()` builds the `BlobServiceClient` from a URL that embeds the full SAS query string, and Azure SDK v12 derived clients inherit that query string. As a result, `getUrl()` returns a base URL carrying the complete account/container SAS signature (`?sv=...&sig=...`), and Apostrophe's `attachment.url()` prepends it to every public attachment link — broadcasting a container-level SAS credential (commonly `sp=rwdlac`, full read/write/delete/list) to every site visitor, including anonymous ones. Anyone who can see an attachment URL can read, overwrite, delete, and list every blob in the container for the SAS lifetime. A companion functional bug (blob path appended after the query string, producing broken URLs) shows this code path was never exercised end to end. Shared-key mode (default) and non-Azure backends are not affected.

Verified at commit `5a3746aaed49761e171c2cbfe793267c959829fd` (uploadfs 1.27.0 in the apostrophe monorepo).

## Details

Root cause: a credential-bearing client URL is reused as the public base URL. The chain:

- Credential-embedded client: [azure.js#L123-L125](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5a3746aaed49761e171c2cbfe793267c959829fd/packages/uploadfs/lib/storage/azure.js#L123-L125) — `new BlobServiceClient("https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net?<SAS query string>")` where `cluster.key` is the full SAS string including `sig`
- Leak point: [azure.js#L513-L520](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5a3746aaed49761e171c2cbfe793267c959829fd/packages/uploadfs/lib/storage/azure.js#L513-L520) — `getUrl()` takes `getContainerClient(...).getBlobClient('').url` as `baseUrl`; SDK v12 derived clients inherit the SAS query string, so `baseUrl` already contains `?sv=...&sig=...`
- Public exposure: [attachment/index.js#L694](https://github.com/apostrophecms/apostrophe/blob/5a3746aaed4

findings.title: ApostropheCMS: Page REST API authorization bypass
findings.summary:
**Summary**
The core page REST API reads full page documents with `.permission(false)` in `getOne` and in the `all=1` tree dump, bypassing page-type `viewRole`, `visibility: private`, and `visibility: loginRequired` checks. **Details**
`packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/page/index.js`:
- `getOne` (L456–465): `await self.publicApiCheckAsync(req); ... self.getRestQuery(req).permission(false).and(criteria)` — no `viewRole` threshold, no `visibility` filtering.
- `all` handler (L318–395): `getRestQuery(req).permission(false)` (L384–385) walks every page type and returns the projection including `visibility`.
- `publicApiCheckAsync` (L3044) only checks that `publicApiProjection` exists — it performs no authorization.
- Correct control behaves differently: `piece-type/index.js:getOne` (L319–327) uses `getRestQuery(req)` without `.permission(false)` and enforces `viewRole`.

**PoC**
```

findings.title: ApostropheCMS: Host header controls server-side image fetch origin in @apostrophecms/ai-helper, enabling authenticated SSRF
findings.summary:
## Summary

The `@apostrophecms/ai-helper` package builds the URL for a server-side image fetch by resolving a storage-relative path against `req.baseUrl`. When the site does not set a global base URL (the default), `req.baseUrl` is derived from the incoming HTTP `Host` header. An authenticated editor can generate a base64 AI image (which is persisted without a stored `url`) and then send an unauthorized `PATCH` accept request with an attacker-chosen `Host` header. The server then issues an outbound `GET` to the attacker-selected origin, producing a Server-Side Request Forgery primitive that reaches hosts and ports the client cannot otherwise contact. The affected code lives in `packages/ai-helper/modules/@apostrophecms/ai-helper-image/index.js`.

## Root Cause

The image accept route trusts `req.baseUrl` as a safe origin for constructing an internal fetch target, but `req.baseUrl` is attacker-influenced whenever the site has no configured base URL. The URL builder concatenates a default local storage path (which is relative, for example `/uploads`) and resolves it against `req.baseUrl`; because the left operand is relative, the resulting origin is taken entirely from `req.baseUrl`. Two protections that exist elsewhere are missing on this path: the generate route enforces an edit capability, but the accept route performs no authorization or ownership check, and no allowlist or validation constrains the resolved origin before the fetch.

  aiHelperFetchImage (line 64-65): fetch(self.aiHelperImageUrl(req, image))
  apiRoutes.patch['ai-helper/:_id'] (line 314-333): findOne({ _id }) only; no permission or ownership check
packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/i18n/index.js

findings.title: ApostropheCMS: Cross-domain session token in URL confers session takeover
findings.summary:
**Summary**
Apostrophe's cross-domain session migration emits a single-use session token as a URL query parameter and stores it in the Mongo cache. Any client that presents the token silently adopts the target user's full session (including `passport.user`) with no credentials.

**Details**
`packages/apostrophe/modules/@apostrophecms/i18n/index.js`:
- Token generation on cross-host/locale flows (L479–487) and passport-bridge cross-locale redirect (`passport-bridge/index.js` L557–593) places the token in the URL.
- `acceptCrossDomainSessionToken` (L258–298) reads `?aposCrossDomainSessionToken`, `Object.assign`s the stored session (cookie + `passport.user`) onto `req.session`, then nulls the cache entry under namespace `@apostrophecms/i18n:cross-domain-sessions`.
- Middleware without `before:` is registered for every URL (express `findModuleMiddlewareAndRoutes` L820–879); verified with `APOS_LOG_ALL_ROUTES=1`.

**PoC**
```
# 0) Anonymous baseline: admin-only draft → 403
# 1) Admin logs in legitimately (token minted into redirect URL):
curl -c admin.cookies -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     --data '{"username":"admin","password":"adminpassword","session":true}' \
     http://localhost:3100/api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login
# 2) Attacker with NO credentials visits the leaked token URL:
curl -c atk.cookies "http://localhost:3100/?aposCrossDomainSessionToken=HUNTING_TOKEN"
#    → 302 Location: / ; attacker now holds a vulnlab.sid SID cookie
# 3) Attacker reads admin-only content via adopted session:
curl -b atk.cookies ".../api/v1/@apostrophecms/page/d576242ve1dkzb12jiiabujd:en:draft"
#    → 200  adopted-session read -> Secret Private Page | secretData = TOP-SECRET-VALUE-abc123
# 4) Cache entry consumed (single-use): {"value":null}
```

**Impact**
Session hijack / account takeover of the migrated user for anyone who obtains the token, inheriting all the account's privileges. Exposure is realistic precisely because the token is in URLs: server/proxy/browse

findings.title: ApostropheCMS: CAPTCHA response token not URL-encoded
findings.summary:
**Summary**
Form and login CAPTCHA verification interpolate the user-supplied widget token unencoded into the server-side verification URL/body, allowing a crafted token to inject query parameters into the reCAPTCHA/hCaptcha verify request.

**Details**
- `packages/form/lib/recaptcha.js:39` — `recaptchaUri = 'https://www.google.com/recaptcha/api/siteverify?secret=${recaptchaSecret}&response=${input.recaptcha}'`
- `packages/login-recaptcha/index.js:44` — same pattern for login
- `packages/login-hcaptcha/index.js:47` — `body: 'response=${token}&secret=${secret}'`

**PoC**
```
input.recaptcha = 'attacker_token&secret=INJECTED_SECRET&something=1'
→ resulting verify URL:
   https://www.google.com/recaptcha/api/siteverify?secret=<real>&response=attacker_token&secret=INJECTED_SECRET&something=1
# (replicated exactly from recaptcha.js:39)
```

**Impact**
Low: a crafted token smuggles extra `key=value` pairs (`secret`, extra `response`) into the outbound verify call, forcing verification failures (DoS of the captcha gate and of captcha-gated login/form flows) and enabling automated bypass probing; no secret exfiltration.

**Remediation** — Build the verify request with `URL` + `searchParams` (or `encodeURIComponent` on both `secret` and `response`), and validate the token against `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,2048}$` before use.

findings.title: ApostropheCMS: Authenticated projection-exclusion prototype-member deletion in @apostrophecms/db-connect causes process-wide denial of service
findings.summary:
## Summary

`@apostrophecms/db-connect` ships an in-memory MongoDB emulation used by its SQLite, PostgreSQL, and multipostgres adapters. Its `unsetNestedField` helper walks an attacker-controlled dotted field path with no segment validation and calls `delete` on the resolved property. A low-privileged authenticated user (any role holding `view-draft`, which every editor and contributor has; reduced to any logged-in user when `guestApiAccess` is enabled) can send a piece-type REST GET request whose `project` query builder contains an exclusion key such as `constructor.prototype.hasOwnProperty`. On a SQLite or PostgreSQL adapter this key reaches `unsetNestedField`, which resolves `Object.prototype` and deletes a shared runtime method. Because that method is shared across the whole Node process, the deletion breaks request handling for every tenant and user until the process is restarted, giving a single request a persistent denial of service.

## Root Cause

The projection query builder laundens only projection values, never projection keys, so an arbitrary dotted key survives to the database layer. On the SQLite and PostgreSQL adapters an exclusion projection is applied in JavaScript by `applyProjection`, which for each excluded field calls `unsetNestedField(result, field)`. `unsetNestedField` splits the field on `.` and walks the resulting segments with no guard: unlike its sibling `setNestedField`, it does not even block a literal `__proto__`, and neither helper blocks `constructor` or `prototype`. Because the working object is a plain object produced by `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(doc))`, its `constructor` resolves to the global `Object`, so a path of `constructor.prototype.<member>` reaches the shared `Object.prototype` and deletes a core, configurable method. The violated invariant is that untrusted input must never be able to traverse into and mutate shared prototype objects.

Affected functions (repository-relative paths):
- unsetNestedField  packages/d

findings.title: @angular/router: Denial of Service via Unmatched Empty-Path Outlet Route Matching in Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
findings.summary:
A denial of service (DoS) vulnerability was identified in `@angular/router` when Server-Side Rendering (SSR) is enabled on Node.js (V8).

During route recognition, `@angular/router` fails to validate whether an auxiliary outlet segment in the URL matches a route configured for that specific outlet name. Because unconfigured empty-path outlet groups (such as `a:/()`, `x:/(...)`, or `///(...)`) are not rejected during matching, the router repeatedly re-evaluates the route configuration against each arbitrary outlet segment provided in the URL.

When a request URL contains multiple arbitrary empty-path outlet segments, this improper matching forces the router to instantiate duplicate `ActivatedRouteSnapshot` trees, repeatedly execute `canMatch` guards and route resolvers, and allocate separate copies of route parameters and `queryParams` for each unconfigured outlet.

An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this behavior by sending requests with crafted outlet segments to exhaust the Node.js memory heap or overwhelm CPU resources, leading to SSR worker termination and service disruption.

### Impact

Successful exploitation allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust the Node.js heap with a single crafted request or a small number of concurrent requests, terminating the SSR worker process with a fatal JavaScript heap out-of-memory crash. When the matched routes declare `canMatch` guards or resolvers, a single short request can also trigger repeated guard or resolver executions, increasing load on backend services and holding worker connections open.

* **Transient Allocation:** Memory is released once route recognition completes; there is no persistent memory leak. The primary impact is process termination.
* **Client-side SPAs Unaffected:** Client-side Angular applications running in the browser are not vulnerable, as browser memory consumption does not cross a security boundary.
* **Prerendering (SSG) Unaffected:** Build-time prerendering does not pro

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ). Implementing the DNS parser in Rust offers
